stem: A city has 200 intersections with traffic lights. The city selected 40 of these intersections at random and installed countdown timers on their pedestrian signals; the other 160 intersections did not get timers. Over the next year, the average number of pedestrian accidents per intersection decreased more at the intersections with timers than at the intersections without timers. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.A: Countdown timers are associated with a greater decrease in pedestrian accidents, but no cause-and-effect conclusion can be drawn because the intersections were not assigned to groups at random.
choices.B: Installing countdown timers would likely cause a greater decrease in pedestrian accidents at intersections in every city in the country.
choices.C: For the city's intersections with traffic lights, installing countdown timers likely causes a greater decrease in pedestrian accidents than not installing them.
choices.D: No conclusion can be drawn because only 40 of the 200 intersections received countdown timers.

solution: Selecting 40 of the 200 intersections at random to receive timers is random assignment of the treatment, so a cause-and-effect conclusion is supported.
All 200 intersections in the study make up the city's intersections with traffic lights, so the conclusion applies to them, but not to intersections in other cities.

explanation.A: Incorrect. The intersections that received timers were chosen at random, which is random assignment, so a cause-and-effect conclusion is supported.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Only this city's intersections were in the study, so the conclusion cannot be generalized to every city in the country.
explanation.C: Correct. The timers were assigned at random among all of the city's 200 intersections with traffic lights, so a causal conclusion about those intersections is supported.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The groups do not need to be the same size; a random group of 40 intersections compared with the other 160 supports a conclusion.

verify:
choices = {o: choices[n] for o, n in {'B': 'A', 'A': 'B', 'D': 'C', 'C': 'D'}.items()}; answer = {'A': 'B', 'B': 'A', 'C': 'D', 'D': 'C'}[answer]  # shuffled: original letters
design = {'random_assignment': True, 'population': "city's intersections"}
assert design['random_assignment']
key = choices[answer]
assert design['population'] in key and 'causes' in key
assert all(design['population'] not in choices[k] for k in choices if k != answer)
